articles.title: Lobster industry caught in Maine’s political headwinds before US midterms
articles.summary: Senator Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson clash over tariffs and their impact on Maine’s economy.
articles.body:
For half a century, day after day, he has taken his boat and headed into the cold waters of the North Atlantic off the coast of the US state of Maine , hauling the crustaceans from the ocean and bringing them ashore. From there, they are loaded onto trucks, sent to processing facilities and shipped to restaurants around the world.

Horner has voted for United States President Donald Trump three times and stands by his vote. He supports the president’s rollback of environmental regulations affecting commercial fishing operations like his own.

While he supports Trump on one policy, however, he’s disappointed in another – the president’s antagonistic approach to Canada, which borders Maine and is deeply entwined with the state’s lobster industry.

“I never heard anything about all this Canadian animosity in the campaign. I don’t know where that came from,” Horner told Al Jazeera. “As far as taking on Canada in this huge hostile trade war, I’m totally against it.”

Horner has watched the price of bait climb along with the cost of the diesel needed to power his boat.

Far beyond Maine’s rocky coastline, tensions involving the US, Iran, Russia and Ukraine have helped drive up global diesel prices, which hit record highs in September. Before the US and Israel began their war on Iran, diesel averaged $3.08 per gallon (3.8 litres) and has now more than doubled to $6.29.

Horner’s business is just one small fish in a very big pond. Maine’s lobster fisheries brought in $461m in 2025, underpinning a seafood economy that is dependent on the crustacean.

But that industry was put on edge when Trump announced sweeping tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa.

In August, Trump imposed tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods while alleging unfair treatment of US products. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs , but lifted the levies on seafood later that month.

Maine’s peak lobster season runs from late summer into early autumn, when catches surge and local processors can struggle to keep up. To handle the volume, much of the catch is sent to Canada for processing into lobster tails, meat and bisque before some of it returns to the US for sale. An estimated 60 percent of Maine’s lobster catch is processed in Canada.

“As soon as those tariffs went out, the screaming, literally and figuratively, in Maine and Canada was quite loud,” Justin Snyder, who works in the Maine lobster industry and is also a Democratic strategist, told Al Jazeera.

While seafood was ultimately exempted from the US-Canadian trade war, the tariff threat raised fears in the industry and put pressure on Susan Collins, the Republican senator who is in a close midterm election race with Democrat Troy Jackson.

The race for the US Senate seat is tight. Jackson, the former president of the Maine State Senate, holds a very slight advantage.

A recent CNN poll suggested Jackson was leading by four percentage points, and a Marist poll indicated he was leading by two points, which is within the margin of error.

Collins has built a reputation in the Senate for voicing concerns about Trump’s policies and rhetoric but supporting his agenda when it comes time to vote. Collins has voted in line with Trump’s position on 92 percent of Senate votes during his second term, which began in January 2025.

However, Collins has broken with Trump on tariffs on several occasions. In April 2025, she voted to overturn tariffs on Canadian goods. Later that month, she supported a resolution to end Trump’s sweeping global tariffs, and in August, she pushed back against the White House over tariffs affecting seafood.

Beyond tariffs on Canadian goods and other imports, levies on foreign steel and aluminium have added costs for Maine’s lobster industry, which relies on the metals to manufacture the traps used by fishermen.

Jackson has been an outspoken critic of Trump’s tariffs, arguing that Collins has not done enough to challenge the president’s trade measures.

During their most recent debate, Collins touted her efforts to secure tariff exemptions for products such as road salt. Jackson pushed back, saying, “We can’t eat road salt.”

Trump removed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods, including certain machinery and packaging products, on October 30, ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. At the same time, his administration extended the tariffs to other Canadian goods, including certain waste products.

“The Canada tariffs are just the dumbest thing in the world. I don’t think there’s anybody up here, Republican or Democrat, who can imagine why we’re involved in this thing,” Maine Republican strategist Lance Dutson told Al Jazeera.

“I don’t think that’s something people are going to point to Susan Collins on, though. I think she’s made it pretty obvious that she’s worked to try to mitigate those things.”

Beyond the immediate costs to Maine businesses, the tariffs risk undermining the competitiveness of US exporters over the longer term.

Trade tensions between Canada and the US have led to Ottawa deepening ties with other countries like China, a move that potentially puts US exporters at a disadvantage.

“Our competitors, namely Canada, are now trading for the most part with those countries tariff-free or with very low tariffs. If we can’t compete with that, we have fewer markets to sell to, which puts downward pressure on the prices paid to fishermen,” Snyder, the Democratic strategist, said.

In China, one of the globe’s biggest markets for lobster, Canadian lobsters face a 7 percent tariff, a significantly lower burden than the 17 percent levied on Maine lobsters.

“They have friendlier trade relations with some of these countries as the US has become antagonistic toward some of its trade partners, giving them a competitive advantage,” Snyder added.

Climate change is also putting pressure on the industry because lobsters thrive in colder waters and are migratory.

Maine remains a major lobster-producing region, but warming waters could keep them moving farther north, making Canadian waters more abundant in the years to come and putting pressure on Maine’s industry.

Jackson has alleged Collins has not done enough to address the underlying causes of heightened prices for Mainers in the lobster industry and beyond, including tariffs.

“Troy spent most of his life working along the Canadian border, so he knows how important this relationship is to Maine’s economy, and he sees Trump’s tariffs for what they are: a tax on Maine families and small businesses,” a spokesperson for Jackson said in a statement provided to Al Jazeera.

The Collins campaign did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.

On the lobster boat, rising costs have made it harder to know whether a day at sea will pay off for Horner.

He plans to vote for Collins, but his support for Trump has grown increasingly complicated. That’s because of high fuel costs and tariffs affecting the cost of goods he uses regularly, leaving his interests at odds with a president who, in other ways, he has seen largely as an ally.

“I wish I could forget about everything else. I would be OK with him,” Horner said. “The high diesel fuel is the biggest enemy of the fishing industry.”

articles.title: Musk is throttling Grok because its cost is 'unsustainably high'
articles.summary: Elon Musk on Sunday said that Grok users would run up against usage limits faster than normal because servicing Grok Bot became too expensive.
articles.body:
Elon Musk said on Sunday that Grok ( SPCX ) users would run up against usage limits more quickly than normal because servicing Grok Bot has become too expensive.

"The cost of serving Grok Bot was unsustainably high relative to revenue," Musk wrote on his social media platform, X.

The sudden throttling highlights one of the biggest questions swirling around the AI revolution: whether demand from users will be enough to sustain a business. It turns out, at least in Musk's case, that demand isn't the problem. The cost is.

Musk was responding to an X user complaining that their Grok Bot usage jumped to 100% before their reset date, when typically they never reached their cap while using the AI agent.

User demand is just one side of the AI market equation, and the businesses churning out sophisticated and expensive models have to — or will have to, eventually — generate revenue to cover their heightened costs. The economics of the still-new and messy AI industry suggest that even healthy demand can't always sustain the AI tools they're selling. Not at these prices — for the users (cheap) and for the corporate compute (expensive; just look at the computing bills ).

That's why the revenue question is increasingly critical and why Musk's admission is so significant. The AI business is running into real-world limitations.

Musk suddenly changing Grok subscriptions so that the AI-usage meter runs faster has struck users and tech observers as unfair and worrisome for SpaceX's business.

"Two weeks ago Grok Bot was an incredible success story powering SpaceXai's revenue growth. Now it's unsustainable and loses money (???)", wrote former xAI worker Benjamin De Kraker in a post on X . Other commenters pointed to a bold and now ironic post Musk sent out a few days ago , saying, "Saving money for the distant future is pointless with the advent of super intelligent abundance."

The tenor of the comments on Musk's own platform, filled with Grok users, turned noticeably sharp : "Yet another Elon rug-pull."

Musk, as he does, is posting through it.

"Just being sensible," he wrote on X , in response to a comment suggesting that investors would punish SpaceX for the decision. In fact, shares are up 5% on Monday. And why shouldn't they be? Wall Street has always loved fiscal responsibility and capitalizing on demand.

Another way to think through the change is that Musk was simply offering an introductory rate to hook users.

Perhaps AI subscriptions are going through their own version of the "VC subsidy," popularized when Uber, Lyft, and other venture-backed apps offered discounts and super-low rates to boost adoption and engagement, only for the apps to sharply increase prices once users became reliant on the services. The classic introductory rate strategy.

articles.title: OpenAI says its AI is getting better at doing things humans do, like shopping and meal planning
articles.summary: OpenAI on Monday announced a new internal tool for assessing how AI handles tasks like these, along with research on how its own models performed.
articles.body: People already use OpenAI’s ChatGPT for things like helping with homework and creating presentations. Now, the tech giant claims its AI models are getting better at everyday tasks largely left up to humans — like shopping and creating a budget. OpenAI on Monday announced a new internal tool for assessing how AI handles tasks like these, along with research on how its own models performed. OpenAI claims its GPT-6 Astra model scored 93.1% at finding the right kindergarten after moving, a 98% score at managing community volunteers preparing for a flood and a 90.4% score at creating a meal plan for a parent recently diagnosed with diabetes. The new benchmark comes at a time when OpenAI faces fierce competition from Meta, Anthropic and Google — all of which are racing to develop AI agents that can handle real-world tasks. OpenAI and its rivals are also grappling with AI safety concerns and pressure to turn a profit from their massive investments in the technology. But first, OpenAI had to come up with a way to figure out whether ChatGPT is actually any good at errands like putting together a grocery cart and filling out online forms. “Because so many people are using the app, we want to capture all the different use cases and the ways that they’re using it, and really understand like how we’re improving over time,” Jenny Yang, a researcher at OpenAI, told CNN ahead of the evaluation’s release. “What are the things that we’re not so good at yet? And how do we just like make this technology better for people?” How OpenAI created the test Standardized evaluations are critical in AI development because AI labs use them as guidance to train and optimize their models to improve in specific areas. Last year, OpenAI released a benchmark called GDPVal to measure how AI performs in work-related skills across industries like manufacturing, government work, finance and sales, among others. The new benchmark could be critical in OpenAI’s push to stay ahead of the competition by turning ChatGPT from a tool for generating content to an assistant that can get things done on users’ behalf. But measuring how AI performs in everyday life presents new challenges. The steps and skills required to adequately shop for groceries or pick out the right kindergarten for a child are broad and vague. And the results can be subjective. Even figuring out what tests to come up with can be difficult because many people use AI differently, and an AI agent’s answers can vary depending on the information it’s given. OpenAI started by looking at broad surveys breaking down how people spend most of their time, like the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ American Time Use survey and the United Kingdom’s Multinational Time Use Survey. The problem, however, was that some of the things that topped the list weren’t tasks that AI could help with, like sleeping or eating. So OpenAI asked ChatGPT users: What kinds of things do you wish an AI assistant could help with? The company surveyed around 4,000 people and had a smaller group of about 100 users write down tasks they wanted AI to do for them, and what personal context they would give the AI model to get the desired result. They also asked the users to come up with a rubric for evaluating whether the AI model successfully completed the task. OpenAI also made sure ChatGPT users had a thorough understanding of the task they were proposing. For example, a person suggesting a test related to how AI handles financial planning should have experience working with a financial advisor for multiple years. Yang said they had a strict list of requirements. “You had to like have evidence that you were some kind of like expert or really understood what the right answer looked like for you,” she said. The tasks that OpenAI is testing can vary widely — from apartment hunting to caring for a loved one. So, what exactly is OpenAI measuring? It’s evaluating the types of skills the model would need to get the right answer, like how well it can navigate websites, apply context by looking at large troves of information in a user’s chat history and make conclusions that align with a user’s needs and expectations. OpenAI’s testing indicates its GPT-6 Astra model, which was released in September, scored 80% on general performance related to prompts involving everyday tasks. Its GPT-5.2 model from December 2025 scored just 49.3%. “There’s just so much information, and a better model would be able to sift through that quickly and really pull out the most relevant pieces,” said Yang. The race to create personal AI agents OpenAI wants ChatGPT to play a more prominent role in everyday life, but it’s facing an onslaught of competitive pressure — particularly from Meta. Meta’s Muse agent, which launched in September, amassed 10 million downloads in the United States in its first 40 days, making it one of the few apps to achieve that milestone, according to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. OpenAI introduced its Dots agent, which it says can work on long-running tasks in the background while users go about their day, within the same month. And Anthropic announced its new AI agent app, Claude Duet, in October. The race to develop personal AI agents also comes as the technology has raised safety concerns following a string of incidents in which AI models broke out of testing environments and breached companies’ systems. Those incidents occurred during testing, not with consumer products, but still raised questions about whether the technology is moving too fast. There’s also the question of whether people will rely on AI too much, and how to draw boundaries when figuring out which tasks to outsource to AI. An anecdote former Yahoo CEO Marissa Mayer shared with The New York Times of how she used AI to summarize what makes her daughter special for a school project drew criticism online. To Yang, the goal is to create AI models that can help people get more time back in their day by either cutting out time-consuming errands — like returning a package or helping them learn a new skill. “I think there’s so many cases like this where being able to use AI just empowers you to do things that you wouldn’t have been able to do, or just makes your life easier overall,” said Yang. “And I think that’s like the main use case that we’re really excited about.”

articles.title: Gas prices likely to drop below $4 a gallon in the next week if oil prices keep declining, analyst says
articles.summary: Gasoline prices are headed below $4 per gallon if oil keeps heading south, says GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan.
articles.body:
Gasoline prices are on track to fall below the $ 4-per-gallon threshold if the Middle East conflict doesn't escalate further and oil prices continue to decline, according to one industry analyst.

On Monday, the national average for gasoline was $4.16 per gallon, about $0.14 lower than a week ago and roughly $0.23 lower than a month ago, according to AAA data.

Over the weekend, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio signaled that President Trump favors negotiations over further attacks on Iran. The country's supreme leader also indicated that Tehran is open to talks, sending oil prices down more than 6%. Brent crude ( BZ=F ) fell to near $105 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) fell to around $97.

"The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum research at GasBuddy, wrote on X on Monday.

The analyst also noted more refining capacity could creep in the months ahead, adding a few thousand barrels per day, or even 10,000 barrels per day.

The move lower marks a reversal of the recent reacceleration in fuel costs as Middle East tensions escalated and inclement weather and constrained refining capacity put upward pressure on prices.

President Trump has said he will not attack Iran before the midterms and has suggested that fuel prices will decline afterward.

Last month, The New York Times reported that the US and Israel had reportedly drawn up plans for renewed attacks on Iran following the Nov. 3 elections. Around that time, the US also ordered nonessential embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia following a series of attacks targeting the country's airports and oil fields.

On Sunday night, Goldman Sachs analysts raised their Brent crude forecast to $105 per barrel for December, up from $90 previously. The analysts expect Brent to average $88 per barrel next year, up from an earlier forecast of $80 per barrel.

articles.title: 'Cannot spill out in public': Sitharaman urges Tata Sons, Tata Trusts to settle dispute soon
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharama on Monday called the differences between Tata Sons and its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, a “very
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharama on Monday called the differences between Tata Sons and its largest shareholder, Tata Trusts, a “very delicate matter” and said both sides should resolve the dispute amicably rather than discuss it publicly.Sitharaman said resolving the matter would require business acumen and cordiality. She also expressed hope that the group's leadership would settle the differences soon.“It cannot be spilling out like this in the public. And for the maturity of that leadership, we would like to have this seen settled sooner,” she said, while speaking at the Financial Express Leadership Awards 2026.Asked whether the government should intervene and bring the two sides to the negotiating table, Sitharaman said the matter required careful handling and declined to comment on possible government intervention.“I think these are very delicate matters, and matters where a lot of commercial and business acumen will have to work. Business cordiality will have to work. So I wouldn't readily say, however serious the issue may be,” she said.Highlighting the Tata group's contribution to the Indian economy, she said the group had built a major global brand and had investments across several sectors.“I know the brand value of Tata, the contribution that the Parsi community has made to make Tata a huge global brand. I also know the expanse of activity in which Tatas are invested in,” she said.“So this is a very critical component to the Indian economy, and therefore it has to be amicably settled among themselves. So they talk it out to make sure that it comes back quickly to some normalcy. It cannot be spilling out like this in public. And for the maturity of that leadership, we would like to have this scene settled sooner. That's the view...” Sitharaman added.What is the Tata Sons-Tata Trusts dispute?Tensions within the 158-year-old Tata group had been building for months before coming out into the open at a Tata Sons board meeting on September 17.The differences involved the board, led by chairman N Chandrasekaran, and Tata Trusts, headed by Noel Tata, the group's largest shareholder.The meeting took place within a week of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejecting Tata Sons' request to deregister as a core investment company.The board decided to proceed with a listing in line with the central bank's mandate and also reappointed Chandrasekaran as chairman.Noel Tata was the only director to vote against the decisions. articles.title: Fox News ratings drop is due to ‘viewer fatigue,’ Murdoch says on eve of midterms
articles.summary: A highly contentious midterm election is contributing to higher ratings for many news brands. But not at the Fox News Channel.
articles.body: A highly contentious midterm election is contributing to higher ratings for many news brands. But not at the Fox News Channel. Fox News remains the most-watched cable channel overall, but its ratings have fallen sharply in recent weeks, prompting speculation that Fox’s Republican-heavy audience is feeling deflated by the midterms. Fox’s own polls have shown Democrats with numerous advantages heading into election night. The network’s base may just be tuning out the news. The year-over-year ratings decline is steep enough that Fox Corp CEO Lachlan Murdoch had to address it when the company released quarterly earnings on Monday morning. Murdoch curiously chalked it up to “viewer fatigue” — though if that’s the diagnosis, it’s unique to Fox, since other news networks are seeing viewership growth. On a conference call with investors and analysts, Murdoch said Fox News as a business “is in incredibly good shape” despite the recent dip. He argued that huge news events in 2025 created a tough “comp,” or comparison, for Fox News this year. He cited President Donald Trump’s inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and interest in DOGE, among other topics. “It was a tremendous news cycle this time last year, which we’re comping against,” he said. “But having said that, we are seeing some viewer fatigue, which we’ve seen before.” Murdoch added: “This cycle is analogous, not entirely, but somewhat analogous to the 2006 midterms, when you have a second-term president going into their midterms halfway after the second term, and you just see this viewer fatigue.” In 2006, it was President George W. Bush, who had an approval rating almost as low as Trump has now. Murdoch said Fox fans “are not going to any other news channel. They’re not switching to MS NOW or to CNN. They’re just, you know, fatigued and watching… slightly less television overall.” Murdoch’s comments about tough comparisons to 2025 are undermined by October ratings, which came out last week. October 2025 was not an exceptionally busy news month. Yet Fox News viewership was down 27 percent year over year while CNN viewership was up 3 percent and MS NOW viewership was up 17 percent. Fox’s contraction and MS NOW’s growth were even more pronounced among 25- to 54-year-old viewers. Overall, Fox scored its lowest audience level in the 25-54 demographic since August 2001. Murdoch told investors that “we’ve seen this playbook” and “know how to move through it.” Fox is used to seeing viewer mood swings show up in the ratings. In 2020, when Trump allies attacked Fox for accurately reporting that he had lost to Joe Biden, Fox’s ratings dropped precipitously. The ratings pressure was on the minds of some Fox hosts and producers who subsequently platformed Trump’s election lies, leading to multiple defamation lawsuits. Emails and texts obtained through Dominion’s defamation lawsuit showed that Fox executives saw the ratings drop as a “brand crisis,” one that necessitated an “All American cookout of hot dogs and hamburgers to get us through.” Over time, the Fox base did tune back in, and Trump reestablished his control over the GOP. This time might be more complicated because the post-midterm period is the effective start of the 2028 presidential primary — one that won’t feature Trump as a candidate.

articles.title: McLaren design boss: First SUV will be 'unmistakably McLaren' as it follows Ferrari, Aston Martin
articles.summary: Kemal Curic hasn't been McLaren's chief design officer for long, but he already knows where he likes to show off its cars: at live events with auto enthusias...
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS — Kemal Curic hasn't been McLaren's chief design officer for long, but he already knows where he likes to show off its cars — at live events with auto enthusiasts in attendance.

"The moment you put them on the lawn, the light, they come alive somehow," Curic told Yahoo Finance at the Wynn Concours in Las Vegas, where McLaren's McL 6GT supercar made its global public debut.

Curic, who previously ran design at Ford's luxury brand Lincoln and led styling on the prior-generation Ford Mustang, joined McLaren this year .

His arrival comes at a pivotal time for the British luxury automaker. The McL 6GT , first seen at a private unveiling at Monterey Car Week in August, pairs a V8 with a manual gearbox — McLaren's first since the F1 in 1992. CEO Nick Collins told Yahoo Finance the production version, due in 2028, will be limited to about 500 cars priced "in the range of $1.5 million."

Curic said the car came straight from clients, who "really wanted something absolutely visceral, emotional, engaging."

But today's luxury buyer is split, according to Curic. On one end are clients who want a tech-laden hypercar like McLaren's W1 — "a piece of F1 technology as a road car," as he put it. On the other are those who want a man-and-machine experience that is "mechanical [and] really visceral."

"There's almost like these two extremes," Curic said. "I would say there are nuances in this new luxury world. I would not say it's just a single luxury element."

The bigger test is McLaren's future. CYVN Holdings, a mobility investor owned by the Government of Abu Dhabi, completed its takeover of the carmaker last year and merged it with its UK startup Forseven under a new parent, McLaren Group Holdings, led by former Forseven boss Collins.

The financial backing was badly needed, as McLaren posted a record £924 million loss ($1.15 billion) in 2023, and its prior owner, Bahrain's sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat, repeatedly injected cash to keep the carmaker afloat.

McLaren will now expand into new product categories, including an SUV . This follows rivals such as Ferrari, Aston Martin, and Bentley into the SUV space.

"You're going to have to be patient with us," Curic said with a smile when asked about a McLaren SUV, though he promised that whatever comes next will be "unmistakably McLaren ... it's going to be executed in our way."

Enthusiasts have been skeptical in the past when sports car makers go the SUV route, but in almost all cases the bigger-footprint vehicles become the brands' top sellers, and profits from those cars subsidize future sportier models.

articles.title: Retirement savers are keen to invest in private assets. Do they know what they're doing?
articles.summary: More than half of investors participating in a workplace retirement plan say they would invest in private equity and private debt if their plan offered them,...
articles.body:
A majority of retirement savers are itching to invest in private assets, a new survey finds.

More than half of investors participating in a 401(k) or similar workplace retirement plans say they would invest in private equity and private debt if their plan offered them, according to investment manager Schroders' 2026 US Retirement Survey.

That's up from 45% in 2025 and 36% in 2024. More than 8 in 10 say they would boost their paycheck contributions to their plan if it offered access to private assets.

Private assets, such as private equity, venture capital, hedge funds, and real estate, are already legal in retirement accounts. However, most plans have been sitting on the sidelines and have not added them yet — for good reason.

Private investments typically come with limited or no ability to sell early, and private funds often carry performance fees and other layers of costs far above what most mutual fund options charge.

"Private assets are moving into the mainstream as regulators and asset managers work to remove the barriers that have traditionally limited access to institutional investors and the ultra-wealthy," Deb Boyden, Schroders' head of US defined contribution, told Yahoo Finance.

Roughly 4 in 10 plan participants now expect private assets to be available in their retirement plan within the next five years, and they are looking forward to that day.

More than three-quarters of people who invest in a retirement plan at work say these investments will offer diversification and better returns than plain vanilla stocks and bonds.

Do they know what they're really getting into? More and more retirement investors say they do. Almost a quarter of plan participants now consider themselves very knowledgeable about private assets, nearly double the 12% who said so in 2025.

"Someone can say they are knowledgeable about private assets, but I would still want to know what they actually understand," said Cary Carbonaro, a certified financial planner and the author of "Women and Wealth."

"Do they understand the liquidity restrictions? The fees? The valuation process? The risk? The time horizon? Do they understand that diversification does not automatically mean lower risk?"

The Trump administration is all in. In response to President Trump's 2025 executive order , the Department of Labor and the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a rule that would allow 401(k) plans to more easily include alternative assets such as cryptocurrency, real estate, and private market assets.

articles.title: Razorpay gets GIFT City licence for cross-border payments
articles.summary: Razorpay secures IFSCA GIFT City licence to offer cross-border payments, multi-currency accounts, and faster integration for overseas investment platforms.
articles.body: Bengaluru: Razorpay has received a final licence from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) to operate as a payment service provider in GIFT City, enabling it to handle cross-border money transfers and support platforms offering overseas investments to Indian residents.The approval follows an in-principle nod in April. The company said its infrastructure in GIFT City, Gujarat’s international financial centre, was ready, with banking connections established with RBL Bank and ICICI Bank. Investment platforms using the service are expected to go live soon. Razorpay said it would add more banking partners.Razorpay said investment platforms seeking to offer foreign stocks typically have to connect separately with banks, remittance providers and systems that check compliance with regulations. Its service would combine these functions through a single connection, reducing the time required for integration from months to two or three weeks.The licence also allows Razorpay to move money in foreign currencies and hold funds in multi-currency accounts, chief operations officer Rahul Kothari said. The company plans to expand its services to include collecting payments from overseas customers, settling transactions and handling other international transfers.“Razorpay already facilitates cross-border payments on both sides: Indian consumers paying global businesses and Indian businesses collecting from customers around the world,” Kothari said. “This licence adds a new dimension to that portfolio.”Razorpay said Indian residents invested $2.65 billion in overseas stocks and debt in FY26, up 56% from a year earlier. It cited the need to work with multiple financial institutions and service providers as a hurdle for platforms seeking to meet this demand.Kothari said the licence could also support transfers by non-resident Indians to their families in India. The final approval adds to Razorpay’s existing regulatory permissions from the Reserve Bank of India for online, offline and cross-border payments.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Internet service providers: TRAI strengthens consumer grievance redressal system; fines upto Rs 20 lakh
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Telecom companies will now have to provide 24x7 consumer support through complaint centres, instead of their existing 16-hour arrangement.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Telecom companies will now have to provide 24x7 consumer support through complaint centres, instead of their existing 16-hour arrangement. Telcos failing to comply with the new rules will face steep fines of upto Rs 20 lakh.The time limit for filing an appeal following disposal of a complaint has been halved from 30 days to 15 and consumers will now be able to do so through the service provider’s mobile application, website or portal also in addition to the existing channels of email, post, in person to ensure faster resolution of appeal. The appellate authority will have to decide an appeal within 15 days of receiving the same.The new rules come in force with the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) on Monday issuing “telecom consumers complaint redressal (fourth amendment) regulations, 2026” applicable to internet service providers having more than 10,000 subscribers.“Complaint centres will be available round the clock on all days of the week, instead of the existing 16-hour arrangement…. Human assistance shall be available for at least sixteen hours daily. Technology-based solutions shall function with appropriate human oversight,” say the new rules.“The appellate authority has been made more responsible through the present amendment. It has been mandated that the appellate authority shall comprise one or more persons who are regular employees in the management of the service provider and also possess at least five years’ experience,” it says. The earlier process of resolution of appeal cases through an advisory committee has been dispensed with in order to ensure efficient and time-bound resolution of appeal cases.“A new mechanism of ‘feedback survey’ has been introduced. Upon resolution or closure of a complaint or appeal, the service provider shall conduct an online feedback survey to assess the consumer’s satisfaction with the resolution. articles.title: Oil prices slide as hopes rise for potential US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough
articles.summary: Oil prices took a leg down on Monday on reports of diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran.
articles.body:
Oil prices took a leg down on Monday as the outlook for potential diplomatic breakthroughs in the Middle East strengthened just a day before midterm elections that could represent a pivotal moment for the Iran war.

Futures on Brent crude ( BZ=F ), the international benchmark, shed around 7.9% to trade below $105 per barrel, while those on US WTI crude ( CL=F ) lost 7.5% to hold near $96.

Oil futures initially began to move downward on Monday after Axios reported that, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pressed the White House for a forceful round of strikes on Iran, President Trump has said he wants to give diplomacy with Tehran another shot .

The reporting from Axios aligns with public statements in recent days from President Trump, where he has said the US won't strike Iran after the midterms. However, reporting by national outlets in recent weeks has indicated that the US military has briefed Trump on options for a major reescalation after the midterms, when the risk of political backlash against the president will be lessened.

Adding to the downward pressure on oil prices Monday, leaders in Tehran said contact with the US over negotiations to end the war is continuing , Reuters reported, as talks between Iran and Qatari mediators have produced proposal language but no breakthrough agreement.

"Consultations through mediators are very intensive," Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in comments to the state-run media outlet IRNA. "We have ‌presented our conditions and proposals and everything depends on the political rationality of Washington."

Leaders in China and Russia both spoke out against a full-fledged resumption of hostilities on Monday, in comments from their foreign ministries. China is a major buyer of energy from the Gulf region, and after largely staying out of the conflict through its first several months, it has engaged more directly in recent weeks.

In Russia, the war in Iran has added to the nation's domestic fuel shortage, caused largely by strikes on oil refineries by the Ukrainian military and international sanctions levied against Moscow. President Vladimir Putin reportedly spoke with Iranian security lead official Mohsen Rezaei on Monday , per Reuters.

Even so, the diplomatic headlines haven't yet tempered predictions on Wall Street that oil prices will remain higher for longer. Goldman Sachs analysts led by Daan Struyven said on Monday that they now expect Brent prices to average $105 per barrel in December, up from a previous forecast of $90. They see Brent contracts averaging $88 per barrel in 2027, up from a prior $80 forecast.

articles.title: US petrol prices dip ahead of midterms as voters eye costs
articles.summary: Diesel prices ease to $6.29 per gallon, offering slight relief amid a global fuel demand squeeze.
articles.body:
Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters.

On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago.

By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran.

Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53.

The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data.

Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend.

“Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. The national average could fall under $4 a gallon in the next week barring a course change.”

Cost-of-living issues remain top of mind for US voters as they head to the polls. An Associated Press-NORC poll last month found that a majority of Americans believe addressing cost-of-living issues should be a priority for Congress, including 78 percent of Republicans and 89 percent of Democrats.

“Once this conflict comes to an end, gas prices will drop drastically, and the Iranian terrorist regime will not have a nuclear weapon,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Al Jazeera. “Protecting America’s national security from threats by a radical terrorist regime that has chanted ‘Death to America’ for 47 years was the right thing to do – and President Trump is the only president who has had the courage to do it.”

Rogers added, “Thanks to the exceptional work of the US military, more oil is now flowing out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran conflict began.”

On Wall Street, oil and gas giant stocks were trending downward in midday trading. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent.

The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. The Nasdaq was up 0.7 percent, the S&P 500 0.6 percent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average 1 percent.

articles.title: AMD to report Q3 results following disappointing showing from Intel
articles.summary: AMD will report its third quarter earnings after the bell Tuesday.
articles.body:
AMD ( AMD ) will report its third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday, giving Wall Street a look at AI chip demand as the market continues to digest a stark sell-off in the AI trade and a disappointing outlook from rival Intel ( INTC ) last week.

Intel reported better-than-anticipated Q3 earnings after the bell Thursday , but provided Q4 revenue estimates of between $15 billion and $16 billion, well below analysts' projections of $17 billion.

The news sent Intel stock plummeting nearly 29% .

The company blamed the outlook on a worse-than-anticipated decline in the PC market.

The industry is contending with two overlapping factors: difficult comparisons to last year, when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, forcing enterprises to purchase newer Windows 11 systems, and the steady increase in PC prices, which is eating into demand.

While AMD generates the majority of its revenue via data center sales, a drop in PC demand would still hurt its bottom line.

For the third quarter, analysts anticipate AMD to report earnings per share of $1.97 on revenue of $13 billion, according to Bloomberg consensus estimates. The company saw EPS and revenue of $1.20 and $9.2 billion, respectively, in the same period last year.

AMD's Data Center arm is expected to see sales of $8.19 billion, an 88% increase from the $4.34 billion it reported last year.

The company's Client business revenue, which includes PC sales, is set to top $3.06 billion, up 11% year over year, but flat sequentially.

AMD's gaming business, however, could take a major hit, with Wall Street predicting a 49% revenue decline to $655 million.

The company's gaming division includes products ranging from PC graphics cards to custom silicon for game consoles. Both categories are facing higher prices due to the ongoing memory and storage shortage, depressing customer demand.

articles.title: Anheuser-Busch CEO leaving to take CEO job at high-end gym chain Equinox
articles.summary: From beer to leading a place that helps burn off the calories.
articles.body:
From getting people to lift a cheap Bud Light to getting them to lift a premium-looking dumbbell — that's the upcoming leadership transition for Brendan Whitworth.

AB InBev ( BUD ) said Monday that Anheuser-Busch's CEO Brendan Whitworth is departing the company, which is the North American arm of AB InBev, at the end of November. Whitworth will assume the CEO position at high-end gym chain Equinox.

Michel Doukeris , the CEO of Anheuser-Busch's parent company AB InBev, will lead the key North America business in the interim until a new leader is announced. Doukeris led the North America business from January 2018 to June 2021. He became CEO of AB InBev in July 2021.

It has been an interesting run for Whitworth in the Anheuser-Busch CEO role over the past five years, to say the very least.

Under Whitworth's watch, Bud Light felt the sales effect of a nationwide boycott and became a political punching bag by those on the right.

The sales pressure began after transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney partnered with Bud Light to create an Instagram post during the March Madness basketball tournament in 2023 endorsing the light beer. Following the post on April 1, 2023, AB InBev saw Bud Light sales tank.

A high-profile CBS interview by Whitworth in June 2023 did little to stem the public fallout.

Bud Light sales have continued to be under pressure, more so some three years later, due to increased competition for light-beer drinkers and softer alcohol consumption among an increasingly health-conscious universe.

On the other hand, the AB InBev North America business is doing OK more broadly.

AB InBev said in its third quarter earnings report it was the top share gainer in total alcohol year to date, with market share gains in both beer and spirits. It says it gained share of total alcohol for 10 consecutive quarters, with beer performance led by Michelob Ultra and Busch Light.

AB InBev shares are up 25% year to date.

"Broadly, we remain impressed with the across-the-board progress and view ABI as increasingly the global leader in [alcoholic beverages]," Evercore ISI analyst Robert Ottenstein wrote in a note. "ABI has an unmatched beer portfolio, now meaningfully augmented by its Beyond Beer offerings, is the leader in eComm and digital tech, and has hard-to-match scale advantages in procurement and media properties. In sum, ABI has all the elements of a +high single digit percentage to +double digit percentage compounder worthy of a 20x+ multiple."

articles.title: Apollo Flexes Underwriting Power With $9.6 Billion ADT Debt Deal
articles.summary: Apollo Global Management Inc. has provided about $9.6 billion of debt commitments to support Thrive Holdings’ acquisition of home security provider ADT Inc.,...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Apollo Global Management Inc. has provided about $9.6 billion of debt commitments to support Thrive Holdings' acquisition of home security provider ADT Inc., one of the starkest examples yet of the firm muscling in on large investment banks' turf.

The alternative asset manager plans to bring in banks to co-underwrite the debt, which would then be sold to institutional investors in the high-yield bond and leveraged loan markets in a syndication process, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing private details.

In addition, Apollo is providing some preferred equity to support the deal, according to a filing.

The leveraged buyout transaction marks the latest example of Apollo taking on roles that used to only be held by the largest investment banks, which typically would provide such bridge financing by themselves. Earlier this year, Apollo demonstrated the extent of its ability to forge bank-like relationships with companies — and move even more quickly — by offering Broadcom Inc. a $35 billion debt deal within weeks.

Notably, Apollo alone provided the financing commitments, according to a statement. That leaves the firm on the hook for the entire $9.6 billion if it unexpectedly can't syndicate some of the debt, which could potentially happen if markets turn volatile. While that outcome is unlikely, few firms can provide such a large commitment all at once on a single transaction.

Representatives for Apollo and Thrive declined to comment while messages left with ADT were not returned. Octus earlier reported some details of the financing.

Thrive announced Thursday that it is buying ADT for about $7.6 billion in equity value, or around $15.3 billion when factoring in the company's existing debt. Formed last year, Thrive Holdings is an offshoot of Joshua Kushner's venture firm Thrive Capital Management.

ADT has about $7.8 billion of existing debt, according to a report Thursday by S&P Global Ratings. The agency said the acquisition is likely to weaken the company's credit metrics and could lead it to lower ADT's BB rating by one notch.

"Given the transaction size and the uncertainty regarding ADT's existing debt, we believe cash flow could be constrained by increased borrowing costs," the report said.

articles.title: Robinhood in ‘Food Fight’ for Anthropic IPO Retail Allocation
articles.summary: Robinhood Markets Inc. is competing with other retail brokerages to fight for access to Anthropic PBC’s mega-IPO.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Robinhood Markets Inc. is competing with other retail brokerages to fight for access to Anthropic PBC's mega-IPO.

The firm fields demand from its clients for access to shares in an initial public offering, then sends it to the company going public and the banks handling the stock sale, Robinhood Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma said Monday in a Bloomberg Television interview.

"It's a food fight out there, so we're going to let our demand speak for itself, and then let the companies decide," Verma said.

When SpaceX went public in June, all eligible customers putting in requests for shares with platforms run by Robinhood and competitors Charles Schwab Corp., Fidelity Investments, SoFi Technologies Inc. and Morgan Stanley's E*Trade were allocated some stock. Leading up to the event, the firms jockeyed for a greater allocation, given that retail clients are often at a disadvantage in accessing pre-IPO companies.

Verma said that SpaceX wanted to allocate around 15% to 20% to retail investors, while Robinhood set aside 20% of is own shares for such clients during its own IPO.

"What we are making sure the companies know is, retail is here, they are a force to stay, and given they're 20% to 25% of the equities market, they should consider a large allocation to retail," Verma said.

Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, filed on Oct. 26 for an IPO slated to occur before the US Thanksgiving holiday later this month. The company disclosed Monday that it plans to spend more than $895 billion in the years ahead.

Apple Inc. has agreed to a $250 million settlement of a class-action lawsuit over how it marketed Apple Intelligence features on certain iPhones, and the claim window is now open.

What the Apple iPhone settlement is about

The plaintiffs allege that "Apple promoted AI capabilities that did not exist at the time, do not exist now, and will not exist for two or more years, if ever, all while marketing them as the breakthrough innovation of the iPhone 16."

articles.title: Lumentum Goes From $1 Billion Spinoff to $115 Billion Takeover
articles.summary: In 2015, executives at the Silicon Valley hardware firm known then as JDSU spun off a division making optical components and commercial lasers, believing the...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- In 2015, executives at the Silicon Valley hardware firm known then as JDSU spun off a division making optical components and commercial lasers, believing the unit would be better off chasing growth opportunities on its own.

When Lumentum Holdings Inc. began trading later that year, it had a roughly $1 billion market value and was reporting quarterly adjusted net income of about $15.3 million. A decade later, the company is generating more than $1 billion of sales in a single quarter, saw $461.1 million of adjusted profits last quarter and is now on track to become one of the largest tech takeovers of all time: On Monday, Marvell Technology Inc. agreed to an all-stock purchase that values Lumentum at $115 billion.

The allure of Lumentum has always been its lasers. Telecom firms have for years relied the San Jose, California-based company for lasers, modules and switches to move data over fiber-optic cables across long distances. With the unprecedented expansion of data centers worldwide to power advanced AI systems, Lumentum's technology has taken on a greater purpose: moving massive amounts of data across chips and servers at incredibly high speeds.

Such demand from AI data centers is now so strong that some of Lumentum's components are "completely sold out" through early 2029, Chief Executive Officer Michael Hurlston said in a Bloomberg interview last month. Customers were already starting to lock in orders for 2030, Hurlston said at the time.

There was only one clear way of jumping Lumentum's line: buy the entire company. As analysts at Wolfe Research put it on Monday, the main rationale for Marvell's historic takeover of Lumentum is "vertical integration" in a now "famously tight" laser market.

Bringing Lumentum's capabilities in-house also stands to turn Marvell into an even more formidable rival against Broadcom Inc., which makes its own laser components. Optical interconnects represent almost half of Marvell's revenue targets for the fiscal year 2031, Wolfe Research wrote, so "making sure they have a secure supply of the industry's highest performance lasers would provide a competitive advantage."

Even so, Marvell shares declined as much as 14% to $168.82 on Monday, and Lumentum was down as much as 19% to $685 in New York, reflecting broader investor concerns about a potential AI bubble. Analysts are also questioning the cost-cutting potential between the two businesses' operations. The anticipated 2028 timeframe for completing the tie-up also suggests gaining clearance won't be easy.

articles.body: MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman has said govt is mindful of concerns among retail investors and equity market participants and will consider calls for policy support to the stock market, even as it seeks to sustain economic growth above 7%.Sitharaman said the tax structure remained unchanged from FY24, when equity markets had seen strong inflows, but circumstances had since changed, with foreign institutional investors (FIIs) turning net sellers and concerns among market participants becoming louder. She said sustaining growth of over 7% required capital and govt was listening to demands for support to equity markets.While govt had focused on developing the bond market over the past few years, she said there were now calls for similar attention to equity markets. "I do not want to say more at this point but I recognise the voice," she said at an event organised by Financial Express on Monday.Sitharaman also said she was seeing a revival in private sector investment, with companies responding to visible demand following the rollout of NextGen GST reforms in Sept 2025. While businesses remained selective about sectors and investment opportunities, she said they were increasingly willing to expand capacity because they could see demand in the market."Industry today has the confidence that I'm able to see demand in the market. I can invest and produce and therefore reach the level which I want to reach," she said. At another event, a fireside chat with Hitendra Dave, chief of HSBC India, FM said govt would continue to drive growth through public capital expenditure while maintaining fiscal discipline. She rejected suggestions that it should loosen spending constraints or disregard fiscal deficits and credit ratings to boost investment.She said public capital expenditure had generated multiplier effects by creating productive assets and encouraging private investment. "Capital expenditure remains a core engine of our growth strategy. Sustained public capex creates productive assets and crowding-in effects for private investment," she said, adding that govt would continue to support economic momentum through high capital spending. FM said fiscal consolidation and growth-inducing expenditure had to be balanced. "We will remain fiscally careful while staying creative and proactive in fostering sustainable economic growth," she said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Darius Khambata to leave Tata Trusts, says ‘independence comes at a cost’
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Darius Khambata, one of Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata's closest allies, will leave the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Sir Ratan Tata Trust
articles.body: MUMBAI: Darius Khambata, one of Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata's closest allies, will leave the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT) when his term ends on Nov 8. In a four-page letter dated Nov 2 to Noel and Trusts CEO Siddharth Sharma, Khambata said he would not seek another term, even though both wanted him to stay. He wrote he was "saddened by the current divide" between Noel and N Chandrasekaran, chairman of Tata Sons, in which the two trusts are majority shareholders.Reappointment needs the consent of fellow trustees, and he said it was "not in my character to seek" it. "That independence comes at a cost," he wrote. He said his stand had at times differed from others, including Noel's.His exit narrows the boards at a tense moment. SDTT will have five trustees: Noel, Venu Srinivasan, Vijay Singh, Neville Tata, Bhaskar Bhat. SRTT will have four: Noel, Srinivasan, Jimmy Tata, Jehangir H C Jehangir.At SRTT, Khambata's term lapses automatically. The Maharashtra Charity Commissioner has barred the trust from changing its board while it investigates alleged breaches of public trust law. SRTT can neither appoint trustees nor renew tenures. At SDTT, reappointment needs unanimous approval, which would prove contentious.The Nov 2 letter is the clearest account of Khambata's thinking. He said he was the first trustee to warn against the Tata Sons listing, calling it "existential" for the Trusts at a May 2025 meeting. He said he drafted the July 28, 2025 resolution, passed unanimously, that reaffirmed opposition to a listing while backing a liquidity solution for minority Tata Sons shareholder, Shapoorji Pallonji Group. The resolution also reposed trust in Chandrasekaran to engage with the RBI on Tata Sons' application for deregistration. Khambata said he did not believe that engagement had been meaningful, much less successful. A second resolution on July 28, 2025, backing a third term for Chandrasekaran as chairman, had since been "overtaken by the astounding events of Aug and Sept 2026," he wrote.He also criticised those who "would decouple Tata Sons from the Trusts", calling the group a "national treasure in which neither limb is meaningful without the other." Khambata wrote that the "sad events" of Sept 17, "a day that will live in infamy", had "sullied Tata Sons' reputation". At the Tata Sons board meeting that day, Chandrasekaran was reappointed chairman for another five years. Noel opposed the move.Khambata defended his vote on Sept 11, 2025, when he joined Mehli Mistry, Pramit Jhaveri and Jehangir in opposing Singh's continuation as a Trusts nominee director on Tata Sons board. The move prompted allegations that the four trustees were attempting a "coup".Khambata had called that "absurd" in a Nov 10, 2025 letter and blamed a media-driven narrative.In his latest letter, he said the Sept 11, 2025 vote was meant to strengthen opposition to any listing and that later events vindicated it. In April 2026, he said, Singh and Srinivasan told the media they favoured listing, despite having supported Trusts resolutions against one. Neither had explained the shift to fellow trustees, he said. That vote preserved Trusts' effective veto at Tata Sons by keeping Noel as their key representative on the board. Under Tata Sons' articles, he said, the veto works by a majority of the Trusts' nominee directors. The Sept 17 event showed how critical that was, he wrote.Khambata said the Supreme Court judgment in Tata Sons v Cyrus Mistry validated the Trusts' special rights in the articles and the special duties of Trusts nominee directors. He said it was now untenable to argue that a nominee director who is a sitting trustee can act against the Trust's interests merely because he also owes a duty to the company.Fault lines within the Trusts have deepened over the past year. Noel, Srinivasan and Singh blocked Mehli's reappointment to SDTT and SRTT in Oct 2025. Jhaveri did not seek another term at SDTT and left in Feb.Khambata said he seconded Noel's appointment as chairman in Oct 2024 and was glad Mehli proposed it despite pressure to defer.Khambata emerged as one of Noel's most important supporters as friction between Trusts and the Tata Sons board grew. People familiar with the matter said his imprint has been visible in Trusts' press releases and correspondence with the Tata Sons board. A senior advocate, Khambata first joined the Trusts in 2014 and resigned in Oct 2016, a day after Cyrus Mistry was ousted as Tata Sons chairman. His second stint began in Nov 2023.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: FM Nirmala Sitharaman weighs in on Tata row: 'Should be resolved amicably, internally'
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday the dispute between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons should be resolved amicably, describing the
articles.body: MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday the dispute between Tata Trusts and Tata Sons should be resolved amicably, describing the salt-to-software conglomerate as a critical component of the Indian economy.In her first public comments on the dispute, she said govt would prefer an early resolution that allowed the group to return to normal functioning. "I know the brand value of Tata, the contribution that the Parsi community has made to make Tata a huge global brand. I also know the expanse of activity in which Tatas are invested in. So, this is a very critical component of the Indian economy, and therefore it has to be amicably settled among themselves," Sitharaman said during a fireside chat organised by Financial Express.FM Nirmala Sitharaman was responding to a question on the govt’s reaction to Congress LOP Rahul Gandhi’s allegations that it was attempting to destabilise the Tata Group.Rahul has accused the Modi govt of attempting to “criminally destroy” the group and treating Indian businesses as political playthings amid the dispute between Tata Trusts, which own the holding company, and Tata Sons, which owns the operating businesses.Sitharaman said the matter required commercial judgement and cordiality between the parties. “I think these are very delicate matters and matters where a lot of commercial and business acumen will have to work. Business cordiality will have to work,” she said. Asked whether govt would intervene, she described the issue as sensitive and said she would not like to comment on it.FM also rejected allegations of govt favouritism towards select corporate groups, pointing out that industrial houses targeted in parliamentary criticism were also welcomed and courted for investment by opposition governed states such as Karnataka and Telangana. On 23% growth in GST collections during Oct, she rejected suggestions that high revenues merely reflected a rise in imports (which had risen 42%). She said most imports comprised essential raw materials and intermediate goods required by domestic manufacturers to meet export demand.The minister also rejected allegations that govt was creating instability or undermining democratic processes. She said opposition parties could not have legitimately won elections and formed govts in Karnataka, Telangana and Himachal Pradesh if elections were compromised or regime changes were possible only through street agitation.She criticised the opposition for holding mock parliaments outside legislatures and walking out of legislative debates instead of using their constitutional mandate. With around 100 elected MPs, she said, the opposition should engage in debates on the floor of the House rather than walk out when govt’s responses challenged its claims.You use AI every day. articles.title: The Intel stock collapse is getting worse — and the $3.7 trillion chip rout is spreading
articles.summary: Intel's slide spread through memory and storage stocks Monday as most of Wall Street moved on from last week's tech sell-off.
articles.body:
Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house.

About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations.

The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended.

Micron ( MU ), Sandisk ( SNDK ), Seagate ( STX ), and Western Digital ( WDC ) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell ( MRVL ) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum ( LITE ) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia ( NVDA ) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6.

Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants.

Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX ( SPCX ) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet ( FTNT ) and CrowdStrike ( CRWD ), which fell with chips.

Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst.

"The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom."

John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening.

"There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia."

Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term " Octoberphobia ," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%.

Next up is AMD ( AMD ), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell , the same day as the midterm vote.

articles.title: Palantir raises full-year revenue outlook as US commercial sales top US government revenue for the first time
articles.summary: Palantir reported Q3 earnings after the bell on Monday.
articles.body:
Palantir ( PLTR ) beat Wall Street estimates on its third quarter revenue and profit on Monday and raised its full-year revenue outlook as the data software company's US commercial business surpassed its US government sales for the first time ever.

Shares of Palantir were volatile in after-hours.

Palantir reported Q3 revenue of $2.313 billion, a 96% increase from the previous year. Wall Street had expected revenue of $2.17 billion, according to Bloomberg data.

Palantir now sees full-year revenue between $8.530 billion and $8.534 billion, topping analyst estimates of $8.2 billion. The company also raised its US commercial sales target to more than $3.559 billion. Adjusted earnings per share of $0.44 also beat consensus estimates of $0.40.

As for the company's explosive business, Palantir CEO Alex Karp said during the earnings call, "We've gone from being the most attractive person in the physics department to being the captain of the football team."

What else you need to know: Palantir stock is up roughly 2% year to date, even as the company has been caught in the recent tech sell-off. The stock weathered headwinds earlier this year after fears of AI disruption hit the entire software complex.

Palantir has frequently pushed back on those concerns, arguing that the enterprise AI market is splitting into two camps: companies paying millions of dollars for model tokens only to receive "AI slop," and those using the company's underlying infrastructure layer.

Palantir's commercial business has accelerated sharply, building on momentum from its historically dominant US government base.

Earlier this year, Palantir's Maven Smart System became an official Pentagon program, cementing a multiyear role across US military AI projects

Wall Street is mostly bullish on the stock, with 30 Buy ratings, 9 Holds, 2 Sells, and a consensus price target of $216 per share.

articles.title: Durigan quer revisar benefícios fiscais em 2027 para reduzir alíquota do imposto sobre consumo do governo federal | G1
articles.standfirst: Reforma prevê manter estável carga tributária sobre o consumo. Assim, como Congresso aprovou um amplo conjunto de benefícios para produtos e setores, alíquota necessária para demais segmentos da economia ficou mais alta.
articles.summary: Reforma prevê manter estável carga tributária sobre o consumo. Assim, como Congresso aprovou um amplo conjunto de benefícios para produtos e setores, alíquota necessária para demais segmentos da economia ficou mais alta.
articles.body:
O ministro da Fazenda, Dario Durigan, afirmou nesta terça-feira (3) que buscará discutir com o Congresso Nacional, no decorrer do ano de 2027, uma revisão dos benefícios fiscais previstos na reforma tributária sobre o consumo.

O objetivo, segundo ele, é reduzir alguns incentivos aprovados a produtos e setores da sociedade para baixar, no futuro, a alíquota da Contribuição Sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS) do governo federal , proposta na semana passada em 11,3% pelo Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) para o ano de 2027.

🔎Entenda: a reforma tributária prevê manter estável a carga tributária sobre o consumo. Assim, como o Congresso aprovou um amplo conjunto de benefícios para produtos e setores com desoneração ou alíquota reduzida, a alíquota necessária para os demais segmentos da economia ficou mais alta.

"É um primeiro número que mantém a carga tributária conforme aprovado pelo Congresso e vai nos dar as condições, de novo, de fazer um debate claro, já mais baixo do que o governo anterior propôs. Para que a gente siga revendo as exceções, os regimes favorecidos, de modo que a gente tenha uma alíquota menor com tempo", disse o ministro a jornalistas.

▶️ Em 11,3%, a alíquota proposta pelo TCU surpreendeu o mercado e as empresas brasileiras. A expectativa era de que a alíquota ficasse próxima de 9,4%, considerando projeções do setor privado e do Comitê Gestor do IBS — o tributo dos estados e municípios sobre o consumo.

O valor proposto pelo TCU será encaminhado ao Congresso Nacional, que poderá concordar ou não. Caberá ao Senado fixar o valor final da alíquota, que será cobrada a partir de 2027, até 15 de dezembro.

Segundo explicou Durigan, o Senado Federal não poderá, neste momento, reduzir benefícios para tentar baixar a alíquota da CBS antes que ela entre em vigor, em 2027, pois os incentivos foram aprovados em proposta de emenda à Constituição (PEC). "Do ponto de vista técnico, não", afirmou.

Dario Durigan — Foto: Washington Costa/MF

🔎A CBS substituirá o Programa de Integração Social (PIS), a Contribuição para Financiamento da Seguridade Social (Cofins) e, também, uma parte do Imposto Sobre Produtos Industrializados (IPI).

🔎PIS e Cofins serão extintos em 2026, enquanto o IPI permanecerá somente para itens produzidos na Zona Franca de Manaus (ZFM) — mas com tributação efetiva somente no resto do país.

Mais de 30% com o imposto dos estados e municípios

Além da CBS do governo federal, a reforma tributária também contempla a cobrança do IBS estadual e municipal, que terá uma alíquota marginal, de 0,1% em 2027 e em 2028.

A partir de 2029, os estados e municípios começam a aumentar, gradualmente, a cobrança do IBS, até 2032. A cobrança integral começa em 2033.

Assim que a alíquota cheia estiver sendo cobrada, estimativas apontam que o imposto sobre o consumo do governo federal, estados e municípios, somará cerca de 28% em 2033 — o primeiro ano com tributação cheia — uma das maiores alíquotas do mundo.

➡️ Junto com a alíquota do IBS dos estados e municípios, que só entra em vigor integralmente em 2033, cálculos indicam que o futuro imposto sobre o consumo brasileiro pode ficar acima de 30%, superando o patamar de países ricos.

➡️O governo federal, por sua vez, alega que, atualmente, os impostos cobrados sobre o consumo no país são ainda maiores, com tributação média de cerca de 34% – mas que há dificuldade em calcular o peso dos impostos pois o sistema é muito complexo, há exceções. Além disso, alguns tributos incidem sobre si mesmos (por dentro, em cascata).

➡️Este modelo "por dentro" torna mais difícil identificar quanto de imposto está efetivamente embutido no preço de um produto ou serviço. Por isso, as notas fiscais trazem apenas uma estimativa "do valor aproximado de tributos". Com a reforma tributária, eles passarão a ser cobrados por fora (aparecerão separados do valor do produto ou serviço).

"A verdade é que a gente nunca soube e agora a gente vai passar a ter um valor transparente [de quanto se paga em imposto sobre o consumo], destacado, de qual é a tributação sobre o consumo no país. Isso vai ajudar, inclusive, nas revisões que a própria emenda constitucional aprovada pelo Congresso nos determina que sejam feitas no futuro", concluiu o ministro da Fazenda.

articles.title: Telecom companies must give 24x7 consumer support: Trai
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Telecom companies will now have to provide 24x7 consumer support through complaint centres, instead of their existing 16-hour arrangement.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Telecom companies will now have to provide 24x7 consumer support through complaint centres, instead of their existing 16-hour arrangement. Those failing to comply with the new rules will face steep fines of upto Rs 20 lakh.The time limit for filing an appeal following disposal of a complaint has also been halved from 30 days to 15. Consumers will now be able to file appeals through the service provider's mobile app or portal in addition to the existing channels of email, post, in person to ensure faster resolution of appeal. The appellate authority will have to decide an appeal within 15 days of receiving the same.The new rules come in force with Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) Monday issuing 'Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal (4th Amendment) Regulations, 2026' applicable to internet service providers having more than 10,000 subscribers.You use AI every day. articles.title: Disney Eyes Thousands of Layoffs, With Managers Asked to Cut 20%
articles.summary: Walt Disney Co. is moving toward thousands of job cuts with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to p...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Walt Disney Co. is moving toward thousands of job cuts with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to people familiar with the matter.

The savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private.

Some of Disney's operations, which range from theme parks, TV network and the movie studio, will be affected disproportionately. Chief Executive Officer Josh D'Amaro aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses, the people said.

The company has promised double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in the current fiscal year.

A representative for Disney declined to comment.

Disney has cut billions of dollars worth of costs and eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with reductions impacting every division including ABC, Pixar, ESPN, the film studio and the experiences unit. The company had 231,000 people worldwide at the end of the last fiscal year.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 1 that Disney was planning a restructuring of its TV division, and cuts at the company's legal and global affairs unit.

Other entertainment companies including Netflix Inc., Sony Pictures Entertainment and Skydance Corp.'s Paramount and Warner Bros. divisions have also cut jobs as revenue from traditional television declines and streaming subscriber growth slows. The also have to cope with more viewers tuning to social media, online videos and streaming services backed by tech giants like Amazon.com Inc. and Apple Inc.

At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, Disney President Dana Walden said that "there is a need to constantly evaluate how you're structured and how big is the organization. Technology set their sights on our business and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that's what we're going to do."
